report.source_text: After returning from the CT scan, the patient’s condition deteriorated within minutes. The oxygen saturation dropped to about 70% and did not recover even with 10 L of O2 administered via reservoir mask. Respiratory exhaustion was imminent. While intravenous Solu-Medrol and Co-Amoxicillin were administered, intubation was initiated, which proved to be extremely difficult due to swelling of the supraglottic soft tissue, although video-guided GlideScope was used. Consequently, the patient went into hypoxaemia and eventually into cardiac arrest. Reanimation protocol was immediately initiated. After even direct tracheal airway access failed, another attempt was made to orally intubate the patient, this time with success. After around 5 min of mechanical reanimation and a total of 2 mg intravenous adrenalin, ROSC was achieved.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 78-year-old woman with hypertensive cardiomyopathy presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of progressive upper airway symptoms including throat pain, hoarseness, painful submandibular swelling, dysphagia, and breathing difficulties. Initial examination revealed trismus preventing adequate oropharyngeal visualization, low-grade fever (37.7°C), tachycardia (118/min), leukocytosis (17.2 g/L), and elevated CRP (125 mg/L). CT neck with contrast demonstrated the thumbprint sign typical of acute epiglottitis with extensive supraglottic and subglottic swelling causing stenosis. Blood cultures subsequently revealed N. meningitidis bacteremia, prompting antibiotic change from Co-Amoxicillin to ceftriaxone 2g every 12 hours. Following the CT scan, the patient rapidly deteriorated with oxygen saturation dropping to 70%, requiring emergent intubation that was extremely difficult due to supraglottic soft tissue swelling despite video-guided GlideScope use. She suffered cardiac arrest with ROSC achieved after 5 minutes of mechanical reanimation and 2mg IV adrenaline. After 11 days of mechanical ventilation, the respiratory situation improved sufficiently to cease ventilation and reverse the tracheostomy. The patient was discharged to a neurorehabilitation facility for neurological impairments resulting from the initial hypoxic event.
